static-1.title: Why a balloon pulls your hair up
static-1.lead: Nothing happened before you rubbed it. After you rub it, everything changes. What passed between the two?
static-1.hook: You have probably pulled off a sweater in winter and watched your hair float up after it. Rub a balloon on your clothes, hold it against the wall, and it stays there instead of falling. No glue, no tape. What went on between the balloon and the sweater while you were rubbing?

predict.q: You rub a balloon on a sweater. What moves across?
opts: The balloon's + moves to the sweater
The sweater's − moves to the balloon
+ and − trade places with each other
Nothing moves across; the properties just change

missions: At the bottom left, check that Show all charges is selected. The sweater and the balloon each have + and − sitting in pairs.
Drag the yellow balloon onto the sweater and rub it slowly, several times. Follow what moves with your eyes.
Let go of the rubbed balloon. It drifts back toward the sweater on its own.
Press Remove Wall on the right, then bring the wall back. What does the balloon do when the wall is there?
Switch to Show charge differences. Matched pairs disappear and only what is left over stays visible.
At the bottom center, pick the two-balloon option - those buttons are pictures of balloons, with no words on them - then rub both and bring them near each other.
static-1.record: After the rubbing, what was left on the balloon and what was left on the sweater? Write down exactly what "Show charge differences" showed you.

explain.body:
The only thing that moved was negative charge (−). The − that was on the sweater went across to the balloon. Not one + moved anywhere.

The + sits locked in the middle of the atom (the nucleus), and rubbing is nowhere near enough to pull it out. The outer −, on the other hand, are held loosely, so they change seats whenever they scrape against another object. That is why − is always the one that moves in any static electricity story. Miss this and the next lessons will all feel confusing.

The result is a balloon with extra −, so it is negative, and a sweater that lost −, so it is positive. They are now opposites, so they pull on each other.

The wall is a different case. The wall carries no net charge. But when the negative balloon comes close, the − at the surface of the wall are pushed back inward and the + are left in front. Nothing arrived or left - the charges only moved seats - and that alone is enough to pull.

static-1.real: The snap you feel grabbing a door handle in winter, the crackle as you take off a shirt, the way dust clings to black clothes more than anything else - all the same thing. When the air is humid, water in the air carries the − away for you, which is why it hardly happens in summer. That is why static only bothers you in the cold months.

quiz.q: After the rubbing, what charge does the sweater carry?
The balloon is stuck to the wall. Is the wall charged?
opts: Yes - that is why it sticks
No - the charges inside the wall only moved seats

static-2.title: The invisible map drawn around a charge
static-2.lead: Put a single charge out in the open. Nothing looks different, but the space around it has already changed.
static-2.hook: Last lesson you watched a balloon pull your hair. But the balloon and the hair never touched each other. How did a force get across a gap like that? Is there something in between?

predict.q: You place one charge and measure the force at several spots around it. How does it come out?
opts: The force stays about the same however far out you go
The force drops at a steady rate as you move away
The force drops very quickly as you move away
Past a certain distance the force suddenly becomes 0

missions: From the tray at the bottom, drag one red +1 nC into the middle of the screen. The moment you drop it, the arrows around it come alive.
Look closely at the arrows. They get smaller and fainter the further they are from the charge. Size and brightness are the strength.
Pull out the measuring tape at the middle right, measure some distance from the charge, and drop a sensor from Sensors at that spot. Fix the arrow length in your mind.
Move that same sensor twice as far out. Is it half as long, or shorter than that?
Add a blue -1 nC facing it, and put a sensor between the two charges.
Pull out the voltage sensor on the right - the crosshair tool that reads in V - and hold it in different places. The closer to the charge, the bigger the reading.
static-2.record: What happened to the arrow when you moved it twice as far out? Write down what you actually saw.

explain.body:
The space around a charge is filled with something called an electric field. The charge does not "shoot" a force across; the charge changes the space around it. Then any other charge that enters that space feels a force.

The arrows are that map. An arrow points the way a positive charge would be pushed, and its length is the strength. That is why arrows are drawn in empty space where there is no charge at all - they are a forecast: "put a charge here and this is the force it will feel."

When you doubled the distance, the arrow did not drop to half. It dropped to a quarter. Three times the distance gives a ninth. This is the inverse square of the distance, the rule you will check with numbers in the next lesson, and gravity follows exactly the same one.

static-2.real: Just before lightning strikes, an enormous electric field fills the space between the cloud and the ground. Lightning is what happens when the air can no longer hold that force and tears open so electricity can run through. Your hair standing on end is a sign that you are inside that field - if you are up a mountain, get low immediately.

quiz.q: If there is no charge at all where a field arrow is drawn, is there a force there?
opts: There really is a force there
There is no force; it marks the force a charge would feel if it came

quiz.q: Triple the distance and the force drops to what fraction?

static-3.title: Double the distance, and the force becomes what?
static-3.lead: Last lesson you guessed it from arrows. This time you check it with numbers. And there is one more thing you can change besides distance.
static-3.hook: Last lesson you moved the sensor twice as far out and the arrow became a quarter of what it was. That is what it looked like - but is it really so? This sim prints the force as a number. And there is one more thing you can change besides the distance: how much charge there is.

predict.q: Leave the distance alone and double just one of the charges. What happens to the force?
opts: It stays the same - the other one did not change
It goes up four times - squared, like the distance

missions: This sim opens on the screen chooser. Press Macro Scale on the left.
There is a ruler lying in the middle of the screen. Drag it against the two objects and set the distance to 2 cm. Write down the force value you get.
Leave the charges alone and stretch the distance to 4 cm. What fraction of the force is left?
Go back to 2 cm, then double only the size of Charge 1 (−4 → −8 μC). The ◀ ▶ beside the value box lets you hit it exactly.
Look at the two figures hauling on the objects. The charges are different, yet they are pulling with the same force.
Under Force Values on the right, choose Hidden. The numbers disappear and only the arrows are left.
static-3.record: When you doubled the distance and when you doubled the charge, how many times bigger or smaller did the force get? Write the two results side by side.

explain.body:
Double the distance and the force becomes a quarter. Double the charge and the force becomes twice as big. The same word "double", two different results.

That is because distance goes in squared and charge goes in as it is. This is Coulomb’s law.

You saw the two figures hauling the objects with ropes. Look closely and both of them are pulling with exactly the same force. You might expect the side with far more charge to feel a stronger pull, but it does not. The two objects always give each other forces of equal size in opposite directions.

Make one of the charges negative and the arrows flip. Like signs push, unlike signs pull. What sets the size of the force has nothing to do with the signs - only the amount of charge and the distance.

static-3.real: This "inverse square of the distance" is not a rule about electricity alone. Gravity does it, loudness does it, the brightness of a lamp does it. Twice as far from a speaker and the sound energy is a quarter; three times as far from a lamp and the brightness is a ninth. Whenever something spreads out in all directions from a single point, this rule turns up.

quiz.q: Double both charges. How many times bigger is the force?
Which one feels the stronger force, the bigger charge or the smaller one?

static-4.title: Move a magnet and electricity appears
static-4.lead: So far electricity made the force. This time it runs the other way - you move a magnet and make electricity.
static-4.hook: Where did the electricity lighting this screen come from? Coal, nuclear, wind, water - the fuels look completely different, but the last step is the same in every one of them. Spin a magnet near a coil. That is it. Can that really be enough to make electricity?

predict.q: You push the magnet inside the coil and hold it still there. What does the bulb do?
opts: Stays lit - the magnet is inside the coil
Gets brighter - it is as close as it can be

missions: Turn on Lock to Axis at the bottom right. The magnet will only move left and right, which keeps the results clean.
Take the magnet and push it slowly into the coil. What does the bulb do?
Hold the magnet completely still inside the coil. This one observation is the whole lesson.
Now run it through quickly. What is different from the slow pass?
Switch Indicator from the bulb to the meter - the one with the needle. The needle swings the opposite way going in and coming out.
Raise Loops from 2 and widen the Loop Area slider. The same speed of movement now gives a different result.
static-4.record: What did the bulb do while the magnet sat still inside the coil? And what was different between moving it quickly and moving it slowly?

explain.body:
Stop the magnet and the bulb goes out. It goes out even with the magnet sitting right in the middle of the coil.

That is because what makes electricity is not the strength of the magnet but the change. Current flows only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing. Hold it still and nothing happens at all, strong field or weak. Miss this and everything else comes out wrong.

That is also why moving faster makes it brighter. Cover the same distance in less time and the change is steeper, and a steeper change makes stronger electricity. This is Faraday’s law.

Switch to the meter and the needle goes one way going in and the other way coming out. That means the current runs one direction while the field grows and the other direction while it shrinks. Keep shaking the magnet back and forth and the direction of the electricity keeps flipping - and that back-and-forth electricity is exactly what arrives at the sockets in your house.

More loops, or wider ones, make it stronger. The coil is taking in that much more of the change in the field.

static-4.real: A power station uses water or steam or wind to spin a magnet. A bicycle light, a wireless charging pad, an induction cooktop - all the same idea. Tap a transit card at the gate and the coil inside the card picks up electricity from the changing magnetic field the gate makes, which is how a card with no battery in it does anything at all.

quiz.q: If you just leave a very strong magnet sitting inside the coil, does electricity keep coming out?
Run the same magnet through twice as fast. What happens to the electricity?

throw-1.title: Throw it sideways and it still falls in the same time
throw-1.lead: Fire a bullet horizontally and drop another from your hand at the same moment, and both hit the ground together.
throw-1.hook: From the edge of a table, just drop one ball while you shove another hard sideways at the same instant. Which one reaches the floor first? Most people say the one you dropped, because the flying one looks like it needs more time to cover all that distance. In fact they land together. Once you see why, the whole shape of a parabola makes sense.

predict.q: From the same height, one ball is simply dropped and the other is thrown hard, horizontally. Which hits the ground first?
opts: It depends how hard you throw

missions: This is the Intro screen. Drag the cannon on the left up and down for height, and set the launch with Cannon Angle and Initial Speed below.
First turn off the Air Resistance checkbox. For now you want the bare rule.
Raise the cannon to about Height 10 m and set Cannon Angle to 0° (horizontal).
Leave Initial Speed at 0 and fire. It just falls. Write down the Time reading at the top.
Now raise Initial Speed to 15 m/s, leave the angle at 0°, and fire. Is the Time the same as before? That is the answer to ②.
Push the speed up to 25 m/s. It goes much further - what does the Time do?
Use the house button to reach the Vectors screen and tick Velocity Vectors → Components. The velocity splits into a horizontal arrow and a vertical arrow.
While it flies, does the horizontal arrow change? What about the vertical arrow? That difference is the whole story.
Turn on Acceleration Vectors as well. It always points straight down, nowhere else.
Work through angles of 15° · 30° · 45° · 60° · 75° and write down the Range each time. Which angle carries it furthest?
Now switch Air Resistance on and redo just 30° · 45° · 60°. Does the furthest angle move?
throw-1.record: Write down the time it took at speeds of 0, 15 and 25. And which angle carried it the furthest?

explain.body:
The answer is they land together. Whether you set the speed to 0 or to 25 m/s, the time was the same.

The reason is that the horizontal and the vertical do not interfere with each other. What you saw on the Vectors screen is the proof.

  • The horizontal arrow - the same length the whole way. Nothing pushes sideways, so the speed does not change.
  • The vertical arrow - grows longer downward. Gravity only pulls down.

Gravity acts downward only. So the time it takes to fall has nothing to do with how fast you go sideways. Going sideways faster takes you further; it does not keep you up longer.

That also explains the shape. Sideways it travels steadily, downward it speeds up as it falls, and putting the two together gives a curve that starts gentle and gets steeper - the parabola from lesson 12.

45° will have gone the furthest. A low angle falls too soon to have the time; a high angle stays up a long while but hardly moves sideways. 45° is where the two balance.

But switch Air Resistance on and the furthest angle drops below 45°. Air fights the forward motion, so staying up longer starts to cost you. That is why the best angle for a real shell or a golf ball is not 45°.

throw-1.real: The arc of a basketball shot, a free kick, the range tables for artillery - all this same calculation. It is also why a plane dropping relief supplies lets go well before the target: the crates fall while still carrying the plane's sideways speed. A long jumper takes off at more like 20° for a different reason - launching high means planting the foot longer, and that costs the run-up speed.

quiz.q: While a horizontally thrown ball is in flight, its horizontal speed is:
With no air resistance, which launch angle goes furthest?
Which way does the acceleration on a flying ball point?

throw-2.title: Fire it the same way and it lands somewhere else
throw-2.lead: Change nothing at all, fire a hundred times, and every landing spot is different. And yet that scatter has a rule in it.
throw-2.hook: Lesson 1 said that once you fix the angle and the speed you can work out where it lands. So what happens if you really do fire the same cannon on the same setting a hundred times? Do all hundred go through one hole? Of course not - the powder, the air, tiny differences in each shell all vary a little. This sim takes that scatter head on.

predict.q: You change nothing at all and fire 100 times. What do the landing spots look like?
opts: Drifting further out the more you fire

missions: Start on the Variability screen. At the top left you choose Orientation · Projectile · Mystery Launcher. The launch settings are hidden and cannot be changed - that is the point of this screen.
Leave it on Single below and fire one shot. One bar of the Histogram at the top goes up a notch.
Change nothing and fire five more times. Do they land in the same spot?
Switch to Continuous and fire dozens of shots. Watch how the bars pile up. That is the answer to ②.
What shape are the bars making? Is it a bell - high in the middle, low at both edges?
Change Bin Width on the left. Same data, but how finely you chop it up to count changes the bars.
Turn on Paths on the right and every flight leaves its trail. See how much they overlap.
Use the house button to go to the Measures screen. Now you can turn on Mean and Standard Deviation.
Turn on Mean and keep firing. The more shots, the more the mean line wobbles and then settles.
Turn on Standard Deviation. It shows the spread as a width. That is the idea from lesson 14.
Switch to the Custom Launcher and make the scatter bigger and smaller yourself.
throw-2.record: What shape did the bars make after dozens of shots? And what happened to the mean line as the number of shots grew?

explain.body:
The answer is spread out around one particular spot. Not scattered anywhere, and not piled on one point either.

The bars will have made a bell - high in the middle, lower toward both edges. This shape turns up constantly in nature: people's heights, exam scores, measurement error, the weight of manufactured goods. Whenever several small causes of variation stack up, you almost always get this shape.

So you cannot predict one, but you can predict the whole. Where the next single shot lands is beyond you; roughly where a hundred of them will cluster, you can say quite accurately.

Lesson 05 told the same story about radioactive decay. You cannot say when one atom will decay, yet the curve for a great many atoms was as smooth as if it were drawn with a ruler. Gather enough things that vary and a rule comes out.

Which means describing the result takes two numbers.

  • Mean - roughly where they cluster
  • Standard Deviation - how widely they spread

Lesson 14 said "the mean alone is not enough", and here it is in the flesh. Two cannons with the same mean but a different spread are completely different cannons. A cannon that never misses and a cannon that sprays everywhere can share a mean.

Remember, too, that changing Bin Width made the bars look different. The data never changed - only how you grouped it to count. That is worth being careful about every time you read a statistical graph.

throw-2.real: What separates archers is not their mean but their spread. Managing screw diameters in a factory, running a vaccine trial across tens of thousands of people, a forecast saying "60% chance of rain" - all of them lean on knowing the whole while not knowing the one.

quiz.q: Fire repeatedly on the same setting and the landing spots:
opts: Spread in a bell around one point

quiz.q: If two cannons have the same mean range:
opts: Their spread can still be different

quiz.q: Changing the Bin Width:
opts: Leaves the data alone and only changes how it is grouped

throw-3.title: You can never get higher than where you started
throw-3.lead: Lose height and you gain speed; lose speed and you gain height. The total stays put.
throw-3.hook: In lesson 1 the ball you threw went up and came back down. It slowed on the way up and sped up on the way down, as if it were trading height for speed. This sim shows you that trade on a skate park. And the trade has one line it cannot cross.

predict.q: On a track with no friction at all, you put the skater at a height of 5 m and let go. How high can the skater get on the far side?
opts: It depends on the shape of the track

missions: Start on the Intro screen. Drag the skater onto the track and they start sliding.
The Energy box at the top left opens collapsed. Press ▸ to open it. Four bars appear: Kinetic · Potential · Thermal · Total.
Set Friction on the right to None. For now you want the trade on its own.
Put the skater on the high side of the track and let go. How do the bars move back and forth?
At the lowest point, check that Kinetic is at its tallest and Potential at its shortest.
What about the Total bar? Does it hold the same height wherever the skater is?
Watch how far up the skater gets on the far side. Does it pass the height you started from? That is the answer to ②.
Turn on the Pie Chart on the right to see the same thing as a circle.
Now push Friction up a little. The Thermal bar starts to grow, and the skater climbs lower and lower.
Check that the Total bar holds steady even with friction on. Nothing vanished - it moved into heat.
Use the house button to reach the Measure screen and move the Reference Height. Every potential energy value shifts with it.
Change Gravity to Moon or Jupiter. Same track, completely different motion.
throw-3.record: With no friction, how did the highest point the skater reached on the far side compare with the starting height? And which bar grew once you turned friction on?

explain.body:
The answer is exactly 5 m. It cannot go higher than that.

The reason is that the Total bar never changes. The energy the skater has is split in two.

  • Potential energy - bigger the higher you are
  • Kinetic energy - bigger the faster you go

Coming down, potential falls and kinetic rises; going up, the reverse. But their sum is always the same. So at the top of the far side, the instant the speed reaches 0, all of the energy is potential again and that value has to match the value at the start. Same potential energy means the same height.

This is conservation of energy, which is another way of saying there is no free energy. It is exactly why a roller coaster can never build a hill taller than its first one.

The Thermal bar growing when you turned on Friction matters just as much. The skater climbed lower each time, yet the Total held steady. The energy did not disappear; it changed form into heat - the same reason a slide leaves you warm.

Energy that has turned into heat, though, cannot be taken back. It has scattered. That is why a real roller coaster has ever lower hills and finally stops.

It is also worth noticing that moving the Reference Height shifted every potential energy value. Potential energy is a quantity that needs a baseline: its value depends on where you call zero, just like distance and displacement in lesson 14. What matters is never the value itself but the difference.

throw-3.real: Roller coaster design sits on this rule, which is why the first hill is the tallest. A dam holding water high to drop it through a turbine, a pendulum swinging back to the same height, an electric car charging its battery under braking - all of them trade between height, speed and heat.

quiz.q: With no friction, the Total energy:
Turn friction on and which bar grows?
Why is a roller coaster's first hill the tallest?
opts: Because it can never climb above its starting height

throw-4.title: When 3 plus 4 is not 7
throw-4.lead: Quantities with a direction cannot simply be added. What you split by hand in lesson 1 becomes a tool here.
throw-4.hook: In lesson 1 you split a velocity into a horizontal arrow and a vertical arrow. A quantity that carries both a size and a direction like that is a vector. Velocity, force, displacement - most of the quantities that matter in physics are vectors. But adding vectors is not like adding numbers. 3 plus 4 need not come to 7.

predict.q: You add a vector of size 3 to a vector of size 4. How big is the sum?
opts: Anything from 1 to 7, depending on the directions

missions: Start on the Explore 1D screen. Drag vectors out of the drawer on the right onto the graph.
Place vector a with length 3 and vector b with length 4, both pointing right.
Tick Sum on the right. The sum vector appears. How big is it?
Now flip b to point left. What happens to the size of the sum?
Write down the sum for the two same direction and opposite direction cases. Those are the two ends of the range in ②.
Use the house button to go to the Explore 2D screen. Now vectors can point any way you like.
Place vectors of size 3 and 4 again and turn one slowly. The size of the sum travels between 1 and 7.
Set the two vectors at right angles. The sum comes to exactly 5 - the 3, 4, 5 right triangle.

In the Components box on the right there are four picture buttons. Choose the bottom right one, the picture with dotted lines dropped onto the horizontal and vertical axes. The vector splits into horizontal and vertical - what you saw in lesson 1.
Tick Values and the θ picture checkbox below it (show angles) to get the size and the angle as numbers.
Of the two picture buttons at the bottom right, choose the one drawn as a fan of angle marks and the grid turns into an angle scale.
throw-4.record: Write down the size of the sum for vectors of 3 and 4 placed in the same direction, in opposite directions, and at right angles.

explain.body:
The answer is anything from 1 to 7, depending on the directions.

  • Same direction - 3 + 4 = 7. The largest it gets.
  • Opposite directions - 4 − 3 = 1. The smallest.
  • At right angles - 5. The 3, 4, 5 right triangle.
  • At angles in between you get values between 1 and 7.

Why? Adding vectors means laying them end to end. Walk 3 paces and then 4 more: go the same way and you end up 7 paces from the start, but double back and you are only 1 pace away. A vector sum is not how far you walked but where you ended up.

So you cannot just add the sizes. The directions have to come along too. The trick that makes this easy is splitting into components.

That is what happened when you chose the picture button with the dotted lines dropped onto the axes and the vector split into horizontal and vertical. Once they are split you can add horizontals to horizontals and verticals to verticals, plainly. The directions have been sorted out, so it is ordinary addition again.

You already used this in lesson 1. Splitting the thrown ball's velocity into horizontal and vertical made it obvious at a glance that the horizontal held steady while only the vertical changed. What you did by hand there, you have made into a tool here.

Working out a slope as rise ÷ run in lesson 12 is the same idea. Handling something slanted by splitting it into horizontal and vertical is the single most useful trick maths and physics share.

throw-4.real: A plane in a crosswind has to angle its nose slightly into the wind to reach its destination, because the real path is the plane's velocity vector plus the wind's. A boat crossing a river, a tug-of-war pulled at an angle, a crane lifting on two cables - all vector sums.

quiz.q: The sum of two vectors of size 5 and 5 is largest when they are:
Add vectors of size 6 and 8 at right angles:
What is good about splitting a vector into components?
opts: You can add horizontals to horizontals and verticals to verticals

wave-1.title: Pull it twice as far and the energy is four times as much
wave-1.lead: The force doubles but the energy quadruples. That mismatch explains a bow, a slingshot and a car bumper.
wave-1.hook: Pull on a spring and it fights back harder the further you pull. Twice the stretch takes twice the force. So far so obvious. But what about the energy that went in? Twice the force suggests twice the energy, and it is not. Without that mismatch you cannot explain "I only pulled it a bit further - why did it fly so hard?"

predict.q: You stretch a spring twice as far. The energy stored in it is:

missions: Start on the Intro screen. In the checkboxes on the right, turn on Applied Force · Spring Force · Displacement · Equilibrium Position · Values.
Move the Applied Force handle at the bottom and note the Displacement (how far it stretched) each time.
Double the force - does the stretch double too? Check it a few times.
Double the Spring Constant and apply the same force. Is the stretch now half?
Look at the Applied Force and Spring Force arrows. Same size, opposite directions.
Use the house button to reach the Energy screen. A Bar Graph and an Energy Plot appear on the right.
Set the stretch to 0.1 m and note the energy. Then stretch it to 0.2 m and note it again. How many times bigger? That is the answer to ②.
Try 0.3 m as well. How many times the value at 0.1 m?
Look at the shape of the Energy Plot. Straight line, or curved?
On the Systems screen, put two springs side by side and then end to end. What happens to the overall spring constant?
wave-1.record: Write down the energy at stretches of 0.1 m, 0.2 m and 0.3 m. And what shape was the energy plot?

explain.body:
The answer is four times. Going from 0.1 m to 0.2 m doubles the force but takes the energy to four times. At 0.3 m the force is three times and the energy nine.

Why the mismatch? Because the force is not strong from the start. As you begin pulling it is nearly 0, and it builds as you go. Energy is that force piled up over the distance, so the distance grows and the force along the way grows too - it gets multiplied twice.

So force is proportional to the stretch (a straight line) while energy is proportional to the square of it (a parabola). The curve in the energy plot is the proof. It is y = ax² from lesson 12, turning up again.

The mismatch matters day to day.

  • Pull a bow a little further and the arrow flies far harder.
  • Double a car's speed and the braking distance goes to four times, because kinetic energy also goes as the square of the speed.
  • A bungee cord stretched only a little further answers back with a much bigger force.

Remember too that Applied Force and Spring Force were the same size in opposite directions. A spring gives back as hard as you pull. Let go and that force drives the object away - which is where the next lesson's oscillation begins.

wave-1.real: Bathroom scales and kitchen scales are exactly this. The spring shortens in proportion to the force on it, and the machine reads that shortening off as a weight. A click pen, a car suspension, a mattress, the mainspring of a watch - all of them use "it gives back what you put in".

quiz.q: Stretch the same spring three times as far. The force needed is:
Stretch the same spring three times as far. The stored energy is:
The bigger the spring constant:
opts: The stiffer it is, so the less it stretches

wave-2.title: Pull it further and it still takes the same time
wave-2.lead: Big swing or small swing, one round trip takes exactly as long. It is the reason clocks could be built at all.
wave-2.hook: Lesson 1 said a spring gives back what you put in. So what happens if you hang a weight and let go? It is pushed back up, overshoots, comes down again - it oscillates. And here is the strange part. A bigger swing has further to travel, so a round trip ought to take longer. It does not.

predict.q: Same spring, same weight. One you pull down only a little, the other a long way. The time for one round trip is:
opts: Longer for the one pulled further
Shorter for the one pulled further
It depends on the spring constant

missions: This is the Intro screen. Drag a mass off the rack on the left and hang it on a spring.
Set Damping on the right to 0. With no friction it keeps swinging.
In the checkboxes on the right, turn on Natural Length and Equilibrium Position. Two reference lines appear.
Hang the 100 g mass, pull it down a little and let go. It starts oscillating.
Take the stopwatch from the top left, time 10 round trips and divide by 10.
Now pull the mass down much further and time it the same way. Is it the same? That is the answer to ②.
Change to the 250 g mass and take the same measurement. Does heavier mean slower or faster?
Leave the mass alone and push the Spring Constant toward Large. What now?
Change Gravity to Moon. The equilibrium position moves - does the round trip time move with it?
Use the house button to reach the Energy screen. The KE · PEgrav · PEelas · Etotal bars trade back and forth.
Push Damping up. The Etherm bar grows and the swinging dies away. That is the story from course 02 again.
wave-2.record: Write down the round trip time for the small pull and for the big pull. And what happened when you used the heavier mass?

explain.body:
The answer is the same for both. Big swing or small swing, one round trip takes exactly as long.

It looks wrong, but there is a reason. Pulling further does mean further to travel. But pulling further also means the spring pushes back harder, so it moves faster by the same measure. The extra distance and the extra speed cancel out in the time.

This property is called isochronism - the period does not depend on the size of the swing. It is why a clock could be built. Galileo is said to have found it timing a swinging lamp in a cathedral against his own pulse. A pendulum like that lamp is only isochronous while the swings stay small, mind you; a mass on a spring holds exactly even for big ones.

So what does set the period? The two things you checked on screen.

  • Mass - heavier is slower. The restoring force is the same but there is more to move.
  • Spring constant - stiffer is faster. It pushes back harder.

Switching gravity to the Moon is the interesting one. The equilibrium position rises but the round trip time does not change. Gravity only moves the centre of the oscillation; the oscillation itself is settled between the spring and the mass.

The Etherm bar growing as you raised Damping is exactly what lesson 3 of course 02 showed. The energy has not gone; it moved into heat, and that is why the swinging dies away.

wave-2.real: A pendulum clock, a guitar string, the bounce of a car, the earthquake design of a building - all of them are the question of what sets the period. It is also why timing matters when you push a swing: a swing has a period of its own, and you have to push on that beat to build it up. Bridges shaking and buildings swaying in resonance disasters work the same way.

Use a heavier mass and the period:
Switch gravity to the Moon and the round trip time:
opts: Stays the same - only the equilibrium position moves

wave-3.title: The wave travels but the string does not
wave-3.lead: In a stadium wave nobody leaves their seat. What moves is not the people but the shape.
wave-3.hook: In lesson 2 a single mass swung on the spot. But what if there is another mass beside it, and they are joined? The first one's swing passes to the second, and on to the third. That is a wave. And it raises the most confusing question there is - when a wave runs to the right, does the string go right too?

predict.q: You shake a string and send a wave off to the right. How does one point on the string move?
opts: It travels right along with the wave
It moves up and down only, staying where it is
It goes round in a circle

missions: At the top left of the screen, choose Pulse from Manual · Oscillate · Pulse.
At the top right set the end to Fixed End, and turn Damping below down to 0.
Press the button at the bottom left to send one pulse. A hump travels off to the right.
Turn on Reference Line on the right and set it anywhere along the string.
Send another pulse and stare at a single green bead on the reference line. Which way does that bead move? That is the answer to ②.
Drop the speed to Slow Motion at the bottom of the screen and walk forward one frame at a time with the step button beside pause - it is much clearer that way.
What happens when the pulse reaches the Fixed End? Watch whether it comes back flipped upside down.
Change the end to Loose End and send another. Does it flip this time?
Change it to No End and the wave leaves without coming back at all.
Now switch to Oscillate for a continuous wave. Take out the Rulers and measure the wavelength (crest to next crest).
Turn Tension down. The wave gets slower and the wavelength gets shorter.
Turn Damping up. The wave gets smaller as it travels.
wave-3.record: Which way did the bead on the reference line move? And what did the reflected wave look like at the fixed end and at the loose end?

explain.body:
The answer is up and down only, staying where it is. The string does not travel one step to the right.

So what is going right? The shape. More precisely, the energy. Each point pulls its neighbour up, that neighbour pulls the next one up, and it is handed along in turn.

Picture a stadium wave. The wave runs right across the stands, but nobody moves sideways at all. They stand up and sit down where they are.

That is what a wave is - the material stays put and only the disturbance travels. Sound is the same. When someone speaks, the air out of their mouth does not fly to your ear; only the vibration is passed along.

What you saw in the reflections matters too.

  • Fixed End - the returning wave comes back flipped. The end cannot move, so the string pulls on the wall and the wall pushes back by the same amount in the opposite direction.
  • Loose End - no flip. The end is free to fly up.

Reflection is why a guitar string makes a note and why a wind instrument has a pitch. Waves coming back from both ends overlap and build a wave that stands still.

Remember also that lowering the Tension slowed the wave down. The speed of a wave is set by the medium. Not by how hard you shake it, but by how tight the string is - which is why tightening a guitar string raises the note.

wave-3.real: A seismic wave crosses the planet without the ground moving anywhere. Sound and earthquakes are both "the material stays, the disturbance travels". Light, radio and wifi need no material to carry them at all, but that story belongs to course 04. Seismometers catching a quake on the far side of the world, and ultrasound looking inside a body, both live off this property.

quiz.q: As a wave goes past, the medium (string, air, water):
A wave reflected from a fixed end:
opts: Comes back the same way up

quiz.q: Raise the tension in the string and the wave speed:

wave-4.title: Every waveform is a sum of sine waves
wave-4.lead: A square wave, a sawtooth - all of them can be built by adding up smooth sine waves.
wave-4.hook: The waves in lesson 3 were smooth ripples. Real sound is not that pretty. A violin and a piano playing the same C sound different because their waveforms differ. So where do the angular waveforms come from? Remarkably, piling up nothing but smooth sine waves produces them. You are going to build one.

predict.q: Can you build a square wave out of nothing but smooth sine waves?
opts: No - sine waves are round and a square wave has corners
Yes - the more you add, the closer it gets to a square wave
A triangle wave yes, a square wave no

missions: This is the Discrete screen. The upper graph is the individual sine waves, the lower one is all of them added together.
Raise only the first (n=1) of the Amplitude handles on the left. One smooth sine wave appears below.
Now raise the second (n=2) as well. The shape below goes out of shape - two waves have been added.
Push the handles up and down at random and get a feel for how the shape below responds.
Choose square from Waveform on the right. The handles set themselves automatically.
How square is the result? Is there still ripple left in it?
Raise the number under Harmonics on the right. More sine waves get added in.
Push Harmonics to the maximum. It gets far squarer. That is the answer to ②.
Turn on Infinite Harmonics at the bottom right and the true square wave is drawn over the top. Compare it with yours.
Try sawtooth and triangle too. Which of them gets close with fewer sine waves?
Under Measurement Tools, turn on Wavelength and compare the wavelength of the first sine wave with the second.
wave-4.record: On the square waveform, what did the shape look like with few harmonics and with many?

explain.body:
The answer is yes - the more you add, the closer it gets. This is what Fourier found, and it underpins nearly every technology that handles sound and pictures today.

How do round things add up to something angular? The trick is overlapping sine waves of different wavelengths. Take the fundamental (n=1), add a third of the wavelength (n=3), a fifth (n=5) - the odd ones only, each at the right size - and in some places they reinforce into a flat stretch while in others they cancel into a sharp turn. That is how a corner gets made. The proof is that choosing square under Waveform drops the A2, A4 and A6 handles to 0.

But a finite number never gives a perfect square wave. Ripple stays near the corners. Add more harmonics and the ripple squeezes in toward the corner, without ever quite going. Only infinitely many make a true square wave.

You have in fact met this idea already.

  • Course 02, lesson 4 - splitting a slanted vector into horizontal and vertical components.
  • Here - splitting a complicated waveform into sine wave components.

Both are turning something complicated into a sum of simple things, because simple things are easy to handle. It is the favourite trick of physics and maths alike.

It connects to the spectrum from course 05, lesson 3 as well. There, light was split by wavelength into a handful of lines; here, a waveform is split by wavelength into a handful of bars. The same work of breaking a mixture into its components.

It is also why instruments sound different. On the same note, which harmonics are mixed in and in what proportion differs, and that blend is what we call timbre.

wave-4.real: MP3 and JPEG are built on this. They break sound and pictures into components and then throw away the components people barely notice to shrink the file. Speech recognition, noise-cancelling headphones, medical MRI, earthquake analysis, even a wifi signal - all of them handle waveforms by their components.

quiz.q: When you choose square under Waveform, the even-numbered handles (A2 · A4):
Why do instruments sound different on the same note?
opts: The blend of harmonics mixed in is different

quiz.q: Why break a complicated waveform into a sum of sine waves?
opts: Simple things are easy to handle
Sine waves are the biggest waves

light-1.title: Cover half the lens - does half the picture go?
light-1.lead: An image is not made at one point of the lens but by the whole lens together. Cover half of it and the picture is still whole.
light-1.hook: Have you ever thrown the view out of a window onto a wall with a magnifying glass? An upside-down image forms. Now what happens if you cover the bottom half of the lens with your hand? It feels as though the bottom of the picture should be cut away. It is not. Get this answer and you have how an image is made whole.

predict.q: You form an image with a convex lens and then cover half the lens. The image:
opts: Just gets dimmer all over, keeping its shape

missions: Start on the Lens screen. The object is on the left, the lens in the middle, the image on the right.
In the checkboxes on the right, turn on Focal Points (F) and Labels. The focal points on either side of the lens appear.
Set Rays at the bottom left to Principal. The three representative rays from the object are drawn.
Watch the three rays pass through the lens and meet at one point. That point is the image.
Now change Rays to Many. There are far more rays. You can see light spreading out in every direction from a single point on the object.
Do all of those rays gather at the very same point? That leads straight to the answer to ②.
Drag the object far to the left. Where does the image go and what happens to its size?
Now pull the object inside the focal point (F). The image goes and a Virtual Image appears. Tick the checkbox to see it.
Change the Focal Length handle. The thicker the lens, the closer the focal point.
Change the object to Light and drag the Screen to where the image forms.
Use the house button to visit the Mirror screen and see whether a concave mirror does the same thing.
light-1.record: When you switched Rays to "Many", where did the rays gather? And what happened when you pulled the object inside the focal point?

explain.body:
The answer is it just gets dimmer all over, keeping its shape.

What you saw on Many is the answer. Light from a single point on the object spreads in every direction and passes through every part of the lens. And the lens brings all of it back to the same single point.

So cover half the lens and the image still forms at that same point, out of the light that goes through the other half. Only half as much light arrives, so it is dimmer - that is all.

You are usually taught to find the image by drawing the three Principal rays. That is a trick to make the drawing easy, not a claim that only three rays exist. The misreading of it is what makes people think covering a lens cuts the picture.

Worth collecting what the object's position does to the image, too.

  • Beyond the focal point - a real image, upside down, forms on the far side. It can be thrown onto a screen.
  • Inside the focal point - the rays never gather; they spread. Extended backward they look as though they meet, and that is the virtual image. It is what you are looking at when a magnifying glass enlarges text.

A virtual image cannot be thrown onto a screen. No light actually gathers there; it only looks as though it does.

All of this treated light as lines travelling straight. Lenses, glasses and cameras are all explained by that picture. But some things are not, and the remaining three lessons are about those.

light-1.real: Cameras, eyes and glasses all work this way. Your lens thickening to look at something near is a way of shortening the focal length, and short-sight glasses are concave to push the focus back. It is also why telescopes are built with big lenses to see faint stars - bigger gathers more light, so the image is brighter.

quiz.q: Why do we draw only three representative rays to find an image?
opts: Because only three rays really pass through the lens
Because it is a trick to make the drawing easy
Because a lens has three parts

quiz.q: Put the object inside the focal point and:
opts: An upright virtual image is seen

quiz.q: Can a virtual image be thrown onto a screen?
opts: No - no light actually gathers there

light-2.title: Hot things change colour
light-2.lead: Heat iron and it goes red, then white. It is how we read the temperature of a star from its colour.
light-2.hook: Lesson 1 treated light only as lines travelling straight. This time you look at where light comes from. Anything with a temperature gives off light - people, stones, everything - though mostly as infrared you cannot see. Get it hot enough and it starts to be visible; get it hotter and the colour changes. Which is hotter, the red one or the blue one?

predict.q: Make an object hotter and the wavelength it gives out most strongly:
opts: Does not move; only the brightness rises
Has nothing to do with temperature

missions: The Blackbody Temperature handle on the right is the one main control in this sim.
Set the temperature low, around 3000 K. The peak of the curve sits over in the Infrared.
Raise the temperature and watch which way the peak moves. That is the answer to ②.
Find the temperature at which the peak comes inside the Visible band.
Turn on Intensity on the right for the total intensity as a number. Double the temperature - how many times bigger is the intensity?
The area under the curve is the intensity. Raise the temperature only a little and watch the area leap.
Press the Earth · Light Bulb · Sun · Sirius A buttons on the right in turn. Note the temperature and the colour of each.
Where is the peak for Earth? Does it come into the visible band?
Where is the peak for the Sun? Compare it with the range your eyes can see.
Look at the small coloured square at the top right of the screen. It tells you what colour an object at that temperature looks.
Turn on Graph Values and Labels and read the peak wavelength off exactly.
light-2.record: Write down the peak wavelength and the colour of the object at 3000 K, 5800 K and 10000 K.

explain.body:
The answer is it gets shorter - toward the blue. The hotter it is, the further the peak moves to short wavelengths.

So the colour runs in this order.

  • Low temperature - the peak is in the infrared and you cannot see it. Human bodies and the Earth are here.
  • Hotter - the peak comes into the visible and it glows red.
  • Hotter still - orange → yellow → white. The Sun (5800 K) is around here.
  • Very hot - it turns blue. Stars like Sirius A.

So a blue star is far hotter than a red one. The opposite of everyday sense, where red on a tap means hot.

What you saw under Intensity is startling too. Doubling the temperature does not double the intensity - it makes it sixteen times bigger, because it goes as the fourth power. A little more heat gives a great deal more light.

One more thing matters here. The peak moves but the curve is always continuous. Fix the temperature and how much comes out at every wavelength is completely settled. That is the exact opposite of the hydrogen spectrum in course 05, lesson 3, which was a handful of lines.

The difference matters. A single atom emits only at set wavelengths, while a hot lump of matter emits at every wavelength continuously. That is why starlight shows dark lines laid over a continuous rainbow - the continuous light from the star's surface, with the atoms outside it eating particular wavelengths out.

And the attempt to explain this smooth curve brought down the physics of a century ago. The theory of the day said the intensity should shoot to infinity at short wavelengths. To get out of it, Planck forced in the assumption that "energy only moves in lumps" - and that was the start of the quantum. The next lesson is that story.

light-2.real: Reading a star's temperature from its colour is basic astronomy. Infrared cameras finding people in the dark, thermal imaging showing how well a building is insulated, a blacksmith judging heat by the colour of iron, the "colour temperature 2700 K" on a light bulb box - all of it sits on this curve.

quiz.q: Which is hotter, a blue star or a red star?
Double the temperature and the total intensity goes to:
Why can you not see the light a human body gives off?
opts: Its peak is in the infrared

light-3.title: Some things brightness cannot buy
light-3.lead: Shine red light as hard as you like and no electron comes out. A feeble violet light and one comes straight away.
light-3.hook: At the end of lesson 2, Planck forced in the assumption that "energy only moves in lumps". It was a fudge. Then five years later, evidence that the fudge was true turned up. Shine light on a metal and electrons fly out - but in a way that simply cannot be explained if light is a wave.

predict.q: You shine red light on a metal and no electrons come out. Turn the intensity up 100 times and:
opts: Still not a single one comes out
None at first, then some after a while

missions: This is the Intro screen. The material chooser is on the left - a combo box with no label above it, showing the name of the metal - and the Intensity and Wavelength handles are at the top.
Set the metal to Sodium and put Wavelength at a long wavelength, over toward IR.
Push Intensity to the maximum. Does the Current value on the right move at all? That is the answer to ②.
Leaving the intensity at maximum, bring Wavelength slowly down toward UV. At what point do electrons suddenly start coming out?
Write down the wavelength at that point. It is this metal's threshold.
Just past the threshold, turn Intensity down. Even very faint, do electrons still come out at all?
Turn on Show Electrons and watch them fly off.
Change the metal to Copper or Platinum. Does the threshold wavelength move?
Use the house button to reach the Energy screen, where you can see how much energy the electrons come out with.
Does a shorter wavelength give the electrons more energy? What about raising the Intensity?
On the Experiment screen, measure the threshold of a Mystery metal and work out what it is.
light-3.record: Write down the wavelength at which electrons began to come out of sodium. And what changed when you raised the intensity, against what changed when you shortened the wavelength?

explain.body:
The answer is still not a single one. Brightness makes no difference whatsoever.

Treat light as a wave and this makes no sense. A wave delivers more energy the harder it hits, so even a feeble light ought to let an electron save up enough energy over time and escape. In fact, however bright and however long, nothing comes.

Instead it goes like this.

  • Wavelength longer than the threshold - not one comes out, whatever the intensity.
  • Wavelength shorter than the threshold - they come immediately, even in very faint light.
  • Raise the intensity - the number of electrons goes up. Their energy does not.
  • Shorten the wavelength further - the energy of each electron goes up.

Einstein's explanation: light is a hail of grains (photons), and the energy one grain carries is settled by the wavelength. To knock an electron loose, one grain has to carry enough energy. Weak grains are useless however many you throw.

Think of throwing balls. To knock over a brick, a ping pong ball will not do. A hundred of them will not do, nor a thousand. One baseball does it at once. Intensity is the number of balls; wavelength is the weight of each ball.

You will have seen that each metal has its own threshold, because each holds on to its electrons with a different grip. Sodium holds them loosely enough for visible light; platinum grips so hard it takes ultraviolet.

This experiment won Einstein the Nobel Prize - this, not relativity. It is the moment lesson 2's fudge turned out to be real.

light-3.real: Solar power is precisely this effect, which is why the wavelengths a panel can use decide its efficiency. Automatic door sensors, the image sensor in a digital camera, night vision goggles, and the reason ultraviolet harms skin while infrared does not - all of them come out of "the energy of one grain".

quiz.q: Raising the intensity of the light changes:
opts: The number of electrons that come out

quiz.q: Shortening the wavelength of the light:
opts: Raises the energy of each electron
Only raises the number of electrons

quiz.q: Why can this not be explained by light as a wave alone?
opts: Because a wave should work if you shine it long enough, however faint
Because a wave cannot pass through metal
Because a wave has no energy

light-4.title: Send them one at a time and the pattern still appears
light-4.lead: You throw grains one by one and a ripple pattern piles up. One grain went through both slits at once.
light-4.hook: Lesson 3 gave you the evidence that light is a grain. But there has long been evidence that light is a wave too - light through two slits overlaps and makes stripes. Natural enough, for a wave. So what if you throw the grains one at a time? One grain can only go through one slit, so there should be no pattern. This sim shows you the answer.

predict.q: You fire light one photon at a time, very slowly, through two slits. After a long while, the screen behind shows:
opts: Just two bands, at the two slit positions
Stripes - the same pattern as a wave gives

missions: This is the Experiment screen. The source is on the left, a barrier with slits in the middle, and a screen on the right.
Check that the particle chooser at the bottom left is on Photons - the buttons carry no label of their own - and set Source Intensity on the left to Max.
Leave Slit Configuration on Both Open. Stripes appear on the screen.
Now switch to Cover Left. The stripes go and one wide smear is left.
Try Cover Right as well - another single smear. Do the two smears simply added together make the stripes?
Go back to Both Open and take Source Intensity very low. Now the photons go one at a time.
Change the detection mode to Hits. A single dot is marked wherever a grain lands.
The first few land anywhere at all. Leave it running a long while. What appears as the dots pile up? That is the answer to ②.
Change the Slit Separation. What happens to the spacing of the pattern?
Change the Wavelength. Do shorter wavelengths pack the stripes closer?
Change the particle chooser at the bottom left to Electrons or Helium Atoms. Matter makes the same pattern.
Turn on Detector Left. If you check which slit it went through, what happens to the pattern?
light-4.record: What appeared as the dots piled up when you sent photons one at a time? And what happened when you watched which slit they went through?

explain.body:
The answer is stripes pile up. Sent one at a time, you still get exactly the pattern a wave gives.

Let us be clear about why that is strange.

  • Each dot lands at one place. It is a grain, all right.
  • But where it lands depends on whether both slits are open.
  • Cover one and the pattern goes, so the grain apparently knows the other slit is open.

There is no way to say it except that one grain went through both slits at once. And yet it arrives at a single point.

Remember that simply adding the two covered-slit smears did not give the stripes. So it is not "half this way, half that way". Something is overlapping, cancelling and reinforcing.

If you tried the Detector it is stranger still. The moment you check which slit it went through, the pattern vanishes. All you did was add equipment, and the result changed. Do not look and it goes both ways; look and it goes one way.

That electrons and helium atoms give the same pattern matters too. It is not only light that is odd - matter is the same. Atoms can behave like waves.

So the question this course opened with - is light a grain or a wave? - has an answer that is neither "both" nor "one of the two". It is something that is neither the grains nor the waves we know, and which looks like a grain or a wave depending on how you measure it.

That is why this counts as the most famous experiment in physics. It does not give you an answer; it shows you that the world is not shaped the way our intuition says. Course 06 picks the story up from here.

light-4.real: Electron microscopes use the wave nature of electrons: the wavelength is far shorter than light, so they see far smaller things. Semiconductor devices, quantum cryptography and quantum computers all stand on this property. The semiconductors we use every day could not be designed without this "strange" physics.

quiz.q: Send photons one at a time and the screen shows:
opts: One dot at a time, and stripes once they pile up
The whole striped pattern from the start

quiz.q: Cover one slit and the pattern:
Run the same experiment with electrons and:
opts: The same stripes as light appear
